summary_html: Findings by **federal/state oversight** (CFSR reviews, OIG audits, child-fatality commissions) can initiate investigations or corrective actions that open CPS involvement.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — national commission on child abuse/neglect fatalities  
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of state systems  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — OIG oversight of HHS/ACF and grantees

primary_citations.citation_text: New Mexico - NMSA 1978 Chapter 32A, Article 4 (Abuse and Neglect Act: 32A-4-3 duty to report, 32A-4-18 custody hearings, 32A-4-19 adjudicatory hearings), CYFD-published Children's Code compilation (2023 text; 32A-4-3 amended 2025 by SB 42)

New Mexico Statutes Chapter 27 - Public Assistance (public assistance and Medicaid programs; CYFD's child-welfare authority is not in this chapter — it is the Children, Youth and Families Department Act, NMSA 1978 § 9-2A-7(D), and the Children's Code, NMSA 1978 § 32A-1-1, per 8.10.3.3 NMAC)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights of Eventyr J.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that clear and convincing evidence supported the findings and that admitting the Citizen's Review Board chairman's testimony about the mother's statements to the Board did not deprive her of due process.
key_cases.relevance: It is the New Mexico decision describing how the substitute care review board process under Section 32A-8-6 feeds monitoring findings back into the court file.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that there was clear and convincing evidence to support the district court's order terminating Respondent's parental rights and that Respondent's due process rights were not violated

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. Section 671(a)(15), confers no enforceable private right on its beneficiaries and creates no implied cause of action.
key_cases.relevance: It explains why federal child-welfare performance requirements are enforced through the Secretary's plan-approval and review machinery rather than private suits.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf

key_cases.case_name: Yvonne L. v. New Mexico Department of Human Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that children in New Mexico state custody had a clearly established Fourteenth Amendment right to reasonable safety measured by the Youngberg professional judgment standard and reversed qualified immunity on that claim, while affirming that 42 U.S.C. Section 671(a)(10) of the AACWA is too vague and amorphous to be enforced under Section 1983.
key_cases.relevance: The plaintiffs' theory was that New Mexico never designated an authority or adopted standards for child care institutions, an oversight failure the court examines.
key_cases.quote: while it does not require actual knowledge the children will be harmed, it implies abdication of the duty to act professionally in making the placements

reporting_details: In New Mexico every person who knows or has a reasonable suspicion that a child is abused or neglected must report it immediately to a local law enforcement agency, to CYFD (Statewide Central Intake, 1-855-333-7233), or, for an Indian child residing in Indian country, to a tribal law enforcement or social services agency, and failing to report is a misdemeanor (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(A), (F)). A finding that a pregnant woman is using or abusing drugs, made pursuant to an interview, self-report, clinical observation or routine toxicology screen, does not alone form a sufficient basis to report child abuse or neglect, and a volunteer, contractor or staff member of a hospital or freestanding birthing center shall not make a report based solely on that finding; notification of a plan of safe care goes to the health care authority and is not a report of abuse or neglect (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(G)–(I), as amended by Laws 2025, ch. 156).
